quickAnswer: Heybeliada and Burgazada sit just before Büyükada on the Princes' Islands ferry route, yet they receive a fraction of its weekend crowds. Visitors find car-free pine lanes, the hilltop Halki Seminary on Heybeliada, the literary Sait Faik Abasıyanık Museum on Burgazada, rocky swimming coves, and relaxed waterfront fish tables within 60 to 80 minutes of central Istanbul.

body.text: Why are Heybeliada and Burgazada calmer than Büyükada?

Most day-trippers stay aboard the ferry until the final stop at Büyükada, leaving Heybeliada and Burgazada noticeably quieter even on sunny weekends. Both islands ban private motor vehicles, rely on small electric municipal shuttles and bicycles, and keep a slower residential rhythm shaped by year-round islanders, fishermen, and summer families.

Heybeliada is the second-largest of the Princes' Islands and feels greener and slightly more varied, with pine forests covering its central ridges and historic naval school buildings greeting ferries at the pier. Burgazada is smaller and more intimate—easy to cross on foot in under an hour—with a compact harbourfront, pastel wooden houses, and a strong literary heritage.

body.text: What can you see at Halki Seminary and Sait Faik Museum?

On Heybeliada, the nineteenth-century Halki Seminary (Heybeliada Ruhban Okulu) crowns Hope Hill inside a wooded monastery compound dating back to Byzantine times. On Burgazada, the [Sait Faik Abasıyanık Museum](https://www.darussafaka.org/en/about-us/our-institutions/museums/sait-faik-abasiyanik-museum) preserves the seaside home of Türkiye's beloved short-story writer, operated by the Darüşşafaka Society.

Reaching Halki Seminary takes a 20-minute uphill walk from Heybeliada Pier through shaded residential streets lined with bougainvillea and timber villas. Visitors can walk the peaceful gardens, view the historic library exterior and church courtyard, and take in wide views over the Marmara Sea. Because visiting hours around religious holidays or restoration work can shift, check locally at the gate before climbing in late afternoon.

On Burgazada, the [Sait Faik Museum](https://saitfaikmuzesi.org/iletisim/) stands just five minutes uphill from the ferry dock at Çayır Sokak No: 15. Open Wednesday through Sunday from 10:30 to 16:30 (closed Mondays and Tuesdays), the wooden mansion displays the author's notebooks, letters, fishing gear, and personal rooms free of charge, offering an intimate window into mid-century island life.
Where are the best swimming coves and waterfront fish tables?

From June through September, both islands offer clear Marmara water away from central city noise. On Heybeliada, swimmers head south to Çam Limanı (Pine Harbour) or Alman Koyu, where pine branches hang close to the water; on Burgazada, walkers follow the coastal road west to Madam Marta Bay and the stone terrace at Kalpazankaya.

Entry to organized beach clubs in Çam Limanı or Ada Beach carries a day-pass fee covering sunbeds and piers, while open rocky spots near Madam Marta Bay on Burgazada remain informal and simple—bring water shoes for pebbles and sea urchins. For lunch or an unhurried sunset meal, Heybeliada's harbour quay offers reliable meze and grilled fish right beside the moored wooden boats. On Burgazada, locals book ahead for Kalpazankaya Restaurant on the western headland, where outdoor tables sit directly above the sunset horizon.
What ferry schedules run from Kabataş and Kadıköy?

Municipal [Şehir Hatları Kabataş–Adalar ferries](https://sehirhatlari.istanbul/en/timetables/domestic-trips/adalar-princes-islands-lines/kabatas-adalar-177) depart regularly from Kabataş on the European side, call at Kadıköy on the Asian side, and then stop sequentially at Kınalıada, Burgazada, Heybeliada, and Büyükada. Additional commuter boats run on the [Adalar–Beşiktaş line](https://sehirhatlari.istanbul/tr/seferler/ic-hatlar/adalar-hatlari/adalar-besiktas-769) and the [Bostancı–Adalar ring](https://sehirhatlari.istanbul/tr/seferler/ic-hatlar/adalar-hatlari/bostanci-adalar-ring-hatti-770).

From Kabataş, expect roughly 60 minutes to Burgazada and 75 minutes to Heybeliada; from Kadıköy, subtract about 20 minutes. Standard Istanbulkart payment works at all Şehir Hatları turnstiles, with current fares listed on the [Şehir Hatları price list](https://sehirhatlari.istanbul/en/price-list). Because Burgazada and Heybeliada sit only 15 minutes apart by ferry, you can easily combine both in a single day if you start by 09:00.

items: Take a morning ferry before 09:30 on weekends to avoid boarding queues at Kabataş and Kadıköy.
Wear comfortable walking shoes; both islands have steep paved hills behind the pier.
Bring swimwear, a towel, and reef shoes between June and September.
Check the last direct return boat to your side of the city before sitting down for dinner.

faq.q: Can you visit both Heybeliada and Burgazada in one day?
faq.a: Yes. Start on Heybeliada in the morning for Halki Seminary and a pine walk, catch a midday ferry 15 minutes west to Burgazada for the Sait Faik Museum, and stay on Burgazada for a late afternoon coffee or sunset dinner.

faq.q: Are bicycles available to rent on Heybeliada and Burgazada?
faq.a: Yes, rental shops operate near both ferry piers. Keep in mind that Heybeliada's back roads have steep climbs, so beginners often prefer walking or using the small electric island shuttles.

faq.q: What days is the Sait Faik Museum on Burgazada closed?
faq.a: According to Darüşşafaka's museum schedule, the Sait Faik Abasıyanık Museum is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays and welcomes visitors Wednesday through Sunday from 10:30 to 16:30.

faq.q: Are there cars or taxis on the Princes' Islands?
faq.a: Private cars and standard taxis are banned on the Princes' Islands. Only electric municipal shuttles (paid with Istanbulkart) and essential service vehicles operate on island roads.

faq.q: Is the ferry ride rough in windy weather?
faq.a: In strong southern winds (lodos), the Sea of Marmara can become choppy and some fast boats cancel while larger Şehir Hatları ferries continue or adjust schedules. Always check live announcements on windy days.
